reviewMethod.methodNotesMd: Reviewed the output contract, resource-assessment rubric, fresh-review framework, the full `SupplyRequest` StructureDefinition report, the resource-review context, and the deterministic aggregate as prior context. I treated behavior findings as directly in scope only when their `affectedResources` include `SupplyRequest`; shared `Resource`/`DomainResource` behavior is considered context only because the assigned resource is neither base artifact.

r4Maturity.effectMd: R4 `SupplyRequest` was FMM 1 / trial-use, so the standards-stability burden is weak and a breaking retirement is not presumptively disproportionate. That softens the case for retaining the resource in R6 core, but it does not erase the operational risk for implementations that used it for supply logistics.

overall.oneLineConclusion: SupplyRequest has no R6 core resource identity, so R4 instances, typed models, endpoints, and searches need a resource-level migration strategy rather than isolated element preservation.

reasoning.thesisMd: The actual migration shape is resource retirement. R4 defines concrete `SupplyRequest`; the supplied R6 ballot core package has no `StructureDefinition/SupplyRequest` and no exact package-index match. Any R4 instance with `resourceType: "SupplyRequest"` therefore fails before element-level compatibility matters. The main work is selecting replacement workflows and preserving audit/source meaning for historical data.
reasoning.migrationShapeMd: `SupplyRequest` was a generic logistics request for medication, substance, or device supply with required `item[x]` and `quantity`, plus supplier, requester, reason, and delivery source/destination fields. R6 has adjacent resources such as `MedicationRequest`, `DeviceRequest`, `NutritionOrder`, `ServiceRequest`, and `RequestOrchestration`, but the reviewed local artifacts do not identify a one-to-one successor. Migration is therefore not a mechanical field rename; implementations must classify records by item domain and business process, then choose target resources/profiles or a legacy compatibility approach.
reasoning.compatibilityLeverageMd: Because the resource identity is gone, preserving individual old element names would not by itself make R4 data valid or usable in R6. The highest-leverage compatibility work is transition infrastructure: authoritative successor guidance, decision tables, compatibility profiles/packages, search and endpoint migration notes, and implementation CapabilityStatement advertising for any retained legacy support. Retaining a deprecated `SupplyRequest` in R6 core would preserve the most compatibility, but for this FMM 1 / trial-use generic resource it is not obviously low-cost because it would keep a retired resource model and its typed/search/REST surface beside more specific request-family resources.
reasoning.lessBreakingAlternativesMd: The plausible less-breaking base design is a deprecated or compatibility-only R6 `SupplyRequest` for at least one release. That would preserve validation, generated classes, route registration, and old search bases for historical data. I do not treat it as a low-cost must-preserve change: it carries governance, duplicate-representation, and implementation-surface costs, and the R4 baseline was low maturity. By contrast, an official migration map or successor decision table is not itself a base-compatible model, but it is standards-review-worthy and comparatively high value because the reviewed artifacts leave implementers to make semantic mapping decisions independently.
reasoning.behaviorImpactMd: The direct HTTP and SearchParameter behavior findings are real for `SupplyRequest`: base endpoint advertisements and search surfaces disappear when the resource disappears. They reinforce the need to audit clients, routes, generated SDKs, tests, and queries, but they are mostly derivative of the same resource-identity retirement rather than independent avoidable breaks. The shared `Resource`/`DomainResource` operation/search findings can affect any implementation stack, but they are not scored as part of the `SupplyRequest` resource-level conclusion.
reasoning.comparisonToDeterministicAggregateMd: I agree with the deterministic aggregate's top-level result: `majorMigrationAlreadyUnavoidable = Yes`, shape `removed-or-replaced-resource`, and compatibility posture `migration-program-dominates`. The independent review adds two qualifications: first, low R4 maturity makes full base retention less compelling; second, migration-program-dominates should not be read as 'nothing to preserve' because explicit successor/search/endpoint guidance still has substantial practical value.
reasoning.uncertaintyMd: Confidence is high that the supplied R6 core package lacks `SupplyRequest`. Confidence is lower on the intended standards rationale, final replacement guidance, and real-world prevalence because no official R4-to-R6 diff note, ballot rationale, narrative migration page, or authoritative ConceptMap/StructureMap was available in the local inputs.

findingConsiderations.title: SupplyRequest is absent from the R6 core package
findingConsiderations.reasonMd: This is the decisive resource-level break. An R4 `SupplyRequest` instance names a resource type that R6 core does not define, so migration is unavoidable for every instance before any local field can be evaluated. A deprecated retained resource would be the compatibility-preserving alternative, but it is not clearly low cost for a low-FMM generic resource apparently retired from core.

findingConsiderations.title: No one-to-one R6 replacement or authoritative migration map was found for SupplyRequest semantics
findingConsiderations.reasonMd: This shapes the migration program: records may need different targets depending on whether they represent medication supply, device provision, nutrition, substance logistics, procurement, or delivery movement. It is not another structural validation rule, but it is standards-review-worthy because lack of an authoritative map raises the risk of inconsistent or lossy migrations.

findingConsiderations.title: R6 model libraries generated from core will not have SupplyRequest runtime support
findingConsiderations.reasonMd: Missing typed classes, resource discriminators, serializers, routes, and search helpers will be highly visible in SDK and server migrations. This matters operationally, but it is derivative of the resource removal rather than an independent standards choice; preserving it would require a retained compatibility resource or non-core shim.

findingConsiderations.title: Search parameters whose only R4 bases were removed resources disappear from the R6 search surface
findingConsiderations.reasonMd: The old `SupplyRequest` search surface disappears along with the endpoint. Existing clients and tests using status, requester, supplier, item, or other SupplyRequest-specific queries need explicit query migration. Search aliases could help only if a clear replacement endpoint and query semantics are chosen, so this is important migration work rather than a separate reason to preserve the retired resource in core.

findingConsiderations.title: The full base CapabilityStatement no longer advertises many R4 resource REST endpoints
findingConsiderations.reasonMd: For `SupplyRequest`, the missing base endpoint advertisement is the REST/API expression of the same resource removal. It should drive audits of generated route inventories and CapabilityStatement-driven clients, but preserving the old route in base would effectively preserve legacy SupplyRequest support.

findingConsiderations.title: R6 core removes the Resource $meta operation
findingConsiderations.reasonMd: This shared Resource-level operation may matter to systems that also store or expose migrated data, but it is not specific to `SupplyRequest` and should not inflate the resource-level conclusion for a retired low-FMM resource.

findingConsiderations.title: R6 invocation matrix changes instance-level Resource $validate request semantics
findingConsiderations.reasonMd: Validation workflow changes are relevant background for migration testing, especially when validating transformed resources, but they apply through the shared `Resource` operation surface rather than through `SupplyRequest` itself.

recommendedNextActions.actionMd: Publish or obtain an explicit migration decision table for R4 `SupplyRequest` use cases, covering medication, device, substance, nutrition, generic logistics, requester/supplier, `deliverFrom`, `deliverTo`, reason, identifiers, and provenance preservation.

Inventory implementation usage of `resourceType = SupplyRequest`, including persisted data, profiles, generated SDK classes, REST routes, subscriptions, search queries, analytics, and conformance tests before choosing R6 targets.

For systems with historical or active SupplyRequest dependence, define an explicit compatibility stance: retain an R4/legacy endpoint, adopt a non-core compatibility profile/package, or transform to selected R6 resources with documented loss/extension handling.
Create end-to-end tests for migrated searches and endpoint discovery, because the `SupplyRequest` search and REST surface disappear unless the implementation advertises local legacy support.

Recheck final R6 package artifacts or official ballot/change notes when available to confirm whether the absence is final and whether HL7 publishes replacement guidance outside the local computable package.

caveats: The reviewed R6 input is ballot4, not a final R6 release.
No official ballot rationale, Jira history, narrative migration page, or authoritative cross-version map was available locally.
Real-world prevalence of R4 SupplyRequest production use was not established from the local inputs.
Shared `Resource` and `DomainResource` behavior findings were considered context only, as required by the resource-review rubric.
